tip: Korean likes to pivot with a fresh sentence: 예약했어요 (yeyakaesseoyo). 그런데 (geureonde)... – 'but' starts sentence two instead of folding into the middle of sentence one.
안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) stretches 되다 (doeda), 'become', into 'it doesn't work' – heaters, plans, phones, anything failing to function. One phrase covers most complaints.
잘못 (jalmot) in front of a verb means you did it wrong: 잘못 봤어요 (jalmot bwasseoyo) = 'saw it wrongly', i.e. misread. It works with almost any verb – hear, press, send.
장 (jang) counts flat things: 사진 백 장 (sajin baek jang) = 100 photos.
-어서 (-eoseo) = so, because; it merges into the stem here: 세서 (seseo) = because it was strong.
께 (kke) is the respectful 'to' for elders: 할머니께 (halmeoni-kke) = to Grandma.
-어 봤어요 (-eo bwasseoyo) on a verb = have tried it: 먹어 봤어요 (meogeo bwasseoyo) = tried eating.
쯤 (jjeum) attaches straight onto the amount: 세 시간쯤 (se sigan-jjeum) = about three hours, so you usually don't need a separate word for 'about'.
편도표보다 (pyeondopyo-boda), 'than a one-way ticket', can lead the whole sentence – 보다 (boda) marks the comparison wherever it sits, so the word order stays flexible.
한 번 (han beon) = one time; written as one word, 한번 (hanbeon) usually means 'give it a try'.
가르치다 (gareuchida) isn't just classroom teaching – 길을 가르쳐 줬어요 (gireul gareuchyeo jwosseoyo) means she 'taught the road', i.e. showed the way. Directions are taught in Korean.
Korean narrates forgetting as two actions: 놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = 'put it down and came'. Where English says 'left it behind', Korean usually strings the two verbs together.
Memories usually arise on their own in Korean – 추억이 생겼어요 (chueogi saenggyeosseoyo), from 생기다 (saenggida), says they 'came into being' rather than that you made them.
Korean has its own words for short spans of days: 하루 (haru) = one day, 이틀 (iteul) = two days. So 이틀 더 (iteul deo) = two more days, with no number-plus-day.
가 보세요 (ga boseyo) is 'try going' – the -아/어 보세요 (-a/-eo boseyo) ending turns a command into a friendly 'give it a try', much softer than a bare 'go'.
써 보세요 (sseo boseyo) = try using it. 쓰다 (sseuda) is one verb for both 'write' and 'use' – context decides which; here it's using the app.
-부터 (-buteo) means 'starting with' – not just for times. 여권부터 (yeogwon-buteo) = 'starting with the passport', i.e. the passport comes first.
하고 (hago) is 'and' for nouns only: 수영복하고 모자 (suyeongbok-hago moja) = swimsuit and hat. It can't join sentences – that takes a verb ending.
만 (man) = only: 반만 (ban-man) = only half.
You stand a plan up in Korean: 계획을 세웠어요 (gyehoegeul sewosseoyo) uses 세우다 (se-uda), 'to stand something up' – buildings and plans take the same verb.
-아/어 볼 거예요 (-a/-eo bol geoyeyo) = will give it a try: 가 볼 거예요 (ga bol geoyeyo) = will try going.
-고 싶어요 (-go sipeoyo) = want to: 다니고 싶어요 (danigo sipeoyo) = want to work there.
붙다 (butda) literally means 'stick': 서류 전형에 붙었어요 (seoryu jeonhyeong-e buteosseoyo) = you stuck to the screening, so you passed.
떨어지다 (tteoreojida) is literally 'fall': 서류에서 떨어졌어요 (seoryu-eseo tteoreojyeosseoyo) = fell off at the document stage. Failing is falling.
-고 있어요 (-go isseoyo) = in the middle of doing: 하고 있어요 (hago isseoyo) = am doing it.
긴장돼요 (ginjang-dwaeyo) is built on 되다 (doeda) 'become' – nerves are something that happens to you in Korean, not something you are.
연락이 오다 (yeollagi oda) = to get a call/message (lit. contact comes).
설명해 주셨어요 (seolmyeonghae jusyeosseoyo) adds 주다 (juda) 'give' to the verb – the explaining was done for you, as a favor. Without it, they just explained.
부장님이 (bujangnim-i) is someone you show respect to, so the verb adds the respect marker 시 (si), merged into 셨: 시작하셨어요 (sijakasyeosseoyo), not 시작했어요 (sijakaesseoyo).
-들 (-deul) marks a plural: 동료들 (dongnyodeul) = coworkers. Korean often leaves plurals unmarked – you add it when the many-ness matters.
